NOTICE
Notice  is hereby given that the Twenty Eighth (28th) Annual General Meeting (“the AGM / 28th AGM”) of the Members of IRB 
Infrastructure Developers Limited (“the Company”) will be held on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, at 11:30 am (IST) through 
Video Conferencing (“VC”) / Other Audio Visual Means (“OAVM”) to transact the following business:
ORDINARY BUSINESS
1.  To consider and adopt the Audited Consolidated Financial Statements for the financial year ended March 31, 2026, 
together with the Report of the Auditors thereon.
2.  To consider and adopt the Audited Standalone Financial Statements for the financial year ended March 31, 2026, together 
with the Reports of the Board of Directors and the Auditors thereon.
3.  To appoint a director in place of Mr. Ravindra Dhariwal (DIN: 00003922), Non-Executive Director who retires by rotation and, 
being eligible, seeks re-appointment and for that purpose to pass with or without modification(s) the following resolution, 
as a Special Resolution:
  “RESOLVED THAT  pursuant to the provisions of Section 152 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the rules related thereto read 
with Regulation 17(1A) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 (including any statutory modification(s) / amendment(s)/ reenactment(s) thereto), Mr. Ravindra Dhariwal 
(DIN: 00003922) who retires by rotation at this meeting and being eligible, offers himself for reappointment and who will 
attain the age of 75 (seventy five) years in September 2027, be and is hereby re-appointed as a Director of the Company 
(Non-Executive, Non-Independent), liable to retire by rotation.”
SPECIAL BUSINESS
4. To consider and, if thought fit, to pass with or without modification(s), the following resolution as an Ordinary Resolution:
  “RESOLVED THAT  pursuant to the provisions of Section 148(3) and other applicable provisions, if any, of the Companies 
Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 (including any statutory modification(s) or re-
enactment(s) thereof, for the time being in force), the remuneration payable to Joshi Apte & Associates, Practicing Cost 
Accountant having Firm Registration No. 00240 appointed by the Board of Directors of the Company to conduct the audit 
of the cost records of the Company for the financial year 2026-27, amounting to ` 3,00,000/- (Rupees Three lakh only) 
p.a. plus applicable taxes and reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses at actuals, if any, incurred in connection with the 
audit, be and is hereby ratified and confirmed.
  RESOLVED FURTHER THAT  the Board of Directors or Key Managerial Personnel of the Company be and are hereby 
authorised to do all acts, deed and things, proper or desirable to give effect to this Resolution.”
By Order of the Board of Directors

Name of the Director Mr. Ravindra Dhariwal (DIN: 00003922)
Date of Birth and Age 74 years
Date of first appointment on 
the boardMr. Ravindra Dhariwal was first appointed to the Board on August 05, 2022, as the 
nominee of Cintra INR Investments B.V.
Qualification An engineer from IIT Kanpur, and an MBA from IIM Calcutta. He was bestowed the 
distinguished Alumni Award by IIM Calcutta in 2013 and also from IIT Kanpur in 2019.
Brief resume & nature of expertise 
in specific functional areasMr. Ravindra Dhariwal is the Co-founder and Chairman of Sagacito Technologies, a data 
analytics company focused on enabling enterprises to unlock growth opportunities and 
maximise their revenues through advance insights and analytics. He also serves as a 
Senior Advisor, Mentor and Board Member of several leading listed and private companies.
Prior to co – founding Sagacito Technologies, Mr. Dhariwal served as the Group CEO 
of Bennett, Coleman & Co. Limited, India’s largest media conglomerate, with diversified 
media platforms including the Economic Times, Radio Mirchi, Times Television Network, 
Times Internet, Times Out-of-Home (OOH) and The Times of India, the world’s largest 
circulated English-language newspaper.
Mr. Dhariwal has also contributed significantly to the global media industry. He served as 
the World-Wide President of International News Media Association from 2011-2013. In 
2014 he was honoured for his outstanding voluntary contribution to World News Media 
sector worldwide.
Prior to joining Bennett, Coleman & Co. Limited, Mr. Dhariwal spent 12 years with PepsiCo, 
where he was the Pepsi’s first employee in India and played pivotal role in launching 
Pepsi brands in India. He was instrumental in building PepsiCo’s beverage business and 
subsequently held leadership responsibilities across India, Africa, and Southeast Asia.
Mr. Dhariwal began his professional journey with Unilever in India in 1977 where 
he worked in India and Australia for over 12 years mostly in Sales and Marketing 
management positions.
Over a distinguished career spanning over more than four and half decade, Mr. Dhariwal 
has built and scaled consumer businesses all over the world. His extensive international 
experience, combined with his deep understanding of diverse markets and cultures, 
has enabled organizations to strengthen customer loyalty, enhance brand equity, and 
achieve sustained business growth.

Item No.3
Mr. Ravindra Dhariwal (DIN: 00003922) age 74 years (seventy 
four), is the Non-Executive and Non-Independent Director of 
the Company liable to retire by rotation. 
He will attain the age of 75 (seventy-five) years in September 
2027, and the continuation of his Directorship will be subject 
to approval by the shareholders by way of a special resolution 
as per Regulation 17(1A) of the Listing Regulations. Hence 
the approval of the Members is sought for the continuation 
of his Directorship on the Board of the Company even after 
attaining the age of 75 (seventy-five) years.
Mr. Ravindra Dhariwal is the Co-founder and Chairman of 
Sagacito Technologies, a data analytics company that helps 
enterprises drive growth through advanced insights and 
analytics. A seasoned business leader with over four and 
a half decades of global experience, he has held several 
distinguished leadership roles, including Group CEO of 
Bennett, Coleman & Co. Ltd. (The Times Group), India’s largest 
media conglomerate, and was the Worldwide President of 
the International News Media Association from 2011 to 2013. 
Prior to The Times Group, he spent 12 years with PepsiCo as 
its first employee in India, playing a key role in launching and 
expanding the company’s beverage business across India, 
Africa, and Southeast Asia. He began his career with Unilever 
in 1977, serving in sales and marketing leadership positions in 
India and Australia. Mr. Dhariwal currently serves as a senior 
advisor, mentor, and board member to several leading listed 
and private companies, leveraging his extensive international 
experience to help organizations strengthen brands, build 
customer loyalty, and achieve sustainable growth.
Mr. Dhariwal has participated actively in the deliberations of 
the Board and has provided strategic inputs and guidance 
on matters placed before the Board. During the financial 
year 2025-26, he has attended 10 out of 10 meetings of 
the Board and also attended Annual General Meeting 
as well as Extra Ordinary Meetings. His attendance and 
participation demonstrate his commitment to discharging his 
responsibilities as a director diligently.
The Board considers his experience in Business leadership, 
Business Development, Consumer and Customer insights, 
Corporate Governance, Risk Management, technology 
and data-led business opportunities to be relevant to the 
Company’s business. Given the scale and complexity of 
the Company’s infrastructure business and considering his 
vast leadership experience, deep industry expertise, and 
valuable contributions as a member of the Board, the Board 
is of the view that his continued association will be beneficial 
to the Company.
The Board, including all the members of the Nomination and 
Remuneration Committee, considered and approved the 
proposal for continuation of his directorship beyond the age 
of 75 years and recommends the resolution set out at item 
No. 3 for the approval of the members.The details required under Regulation 36(3) of the Listing 
Regulations and Secretarial Standards on General Meetings 
(SS-2) issued by the Institute of Company Secretaries of India, 
in respect of Director(s) seeking appointment/re-appointment 
at this AGM forms part of the Notice.
Except Mr. Ravindra Dhariwal, being an appointee, or his 
immediate relatives, none of the Directors/ Key Managerial 
Personnel of the Company and their relatives is in any 
way, concerned or interested financially or otherwise, in 
Resolution No. 3 as contained in the Notice for the approval 
of the members.
The Board of Directors recommends the Special Resolution 
set out at Item No. 3 of the Notice for approval by the Members.
Item No.4
The Board of Directors of the Company has appointed Joshi 
Apte & Associates, Practicing Cost Accountant, to conduct 
the audit of the cost records of the Company for the financial 
year 2026-27. In terms of the provisions of Section 148(3) 
of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 14(a)(ii) of the 
Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, the remuneration 
payable to the Cost Auditor is to be ratified by the Members 
of the Company. The remuneration of ` 3,00,000/- (Rupees 
Three lakh only) per annum is payable to Joshi Apte & 
Associates, Practicing Cost Accountant, for the audit to 
be conducted for financial year 2026-27. Accordingly, the 
Members are requested to ratify the remuneration payable 
to the Cost Auditors for the audit to be conducted for  
financial year 2026-27.
None of the Directors, Key Managerial Personnel of the 
Company and their relatives, are in any way concerned or 
interested, financial or otherwise, in the said Resolution.
The Board of Directors recommends the Ordinary 
Resolution set out at Item No. 4 of the Notice for approval by 
the shareholders.

NOTES
1.  Explanatory Statement pursuant to Section 102 read with 
Section 110 of the Companies Act, 2013 (the “Act”) and 
the Rule 20 and Rule 22 of the Companies (Management 
and Administration) Rules, 2014, as amended, setting 
out material facts relating to the resolutions proposed 
to be passed is annexed hereto.
2.  The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (‘MCA’), vide its General 
Circular No. 03/2025 dated September 22, 2025, (in 
continuation with the Circulars issued earlier in this 
regard) (‘MCA Circulars’), has allowed the Companies 
to conduct the Annual General Meeting (AGM) through 
Video Conferencing or Other Audio-Visual Means (‘VC/
OAVM’) without the physical presence of Members. In 
compliance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 
2013 (“Act”), SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“Listing Regulations”) 
and MCA Circulars, the AGM of the Company is being 
held through VC/OAVM.
3.  The Company has enabled the Members to participate 
at the AGM through the VC/OAVM facility provided by 
KFin Technologies Limited, Registrar and Share Transfer 
Agents (“KFintech / RTA”). The Members can join the 
AGM in the VC/OAVM mode 15 minutes before the 
scheduled time of the commencement of the Meeting. 
The instructions for participation by Members are given 
in the subsequent pages. Participation at the AGM 
through VC shall be allowed on a first-come-first-served 
basis for first 1,000 members. This will not include 
large Members (Members holding 2% or more equity 
shares), Promoters, Institutional Investors, Directors, 
Key Managerial Personnel, the Chairpersons of the 
Audit Committee, Stakeholders Relationship Committee, 
Auditors etc. who are allowed to attend the AGM without 
restriction on account of first-come-first-served basis. 
The members can visit https://emeetings.kfintech.com  
and login through existing user id and password to 
attend the live proceedings of the AGM of the Company.
4.  Members may note that pursuant to the provisions of MCA 
and SEBI Circulars, the Annual report for the financial 
year 2025-26 and AGM Notice (including remote e-voting 
instructions) is being sent to Members electronically. 
Accordingly, the Annual Report for the financial year 
2025-26 and AGM Notice are being sent only to those 
members whose names appear in the Register of 
Members / List of Beneficial Owners as on August 21, 
2026, received from the Depositories and whose e-mail 
addresses are registered with the Company or with the 
depository participant / depository. Members may note 
that the Annual Report for the financial year 2025-26 
and AGM Notice will also be available on the Company’s 
website at www.irb.co.in , websites of Stock Exchange(s) 
i.e. BSE Limited and National Stock Exchange of India 
Limited at www.bseindia.com  and www.nseindia.com  respectively and on the website of KFintech at https://
evoting.kfintech.com/ .
5.  As per the Circulars mentioned above, the Members may 
also note that the Company would not be sending the 
Annual Report for the financial year 2025-26 and AGM 
notice by post to the Members whose e-mail address 
is not registered with the Company or depository 
participants/depository.
6.  The Company is providing a facility to the members 
as on the cut-off date, being Tuesday, September 15, 
2026 (“the cut-off date”) to exercise their right to vote 
on the matters listed in the Notice by electronic voting 
systems (Remote e-voting). Additionally, the members 
can also exercise their right to vote by e-voting during 
the AGM. The process and manner of remote e-voting 
with necessary User ID and password is given below. 
Such remote e-voting facility is in addition to voting that 
will take place at the AGM being held through VC/OAVM. 
Any person who acquires shares of the Company and 
becomes a Member of the company after the dispatch 
of the Notice, and holding shares as on the cut-off date, 
may obtain the User ID and Password by sending a 
request at evoting@kfintech.com  or contact KFintech at 
toll free number 1-800-309-4001. Voting by electronic 
mode is a convenient means of exercising voting rights 
and may help to increase the member’s participation in 
the decision-making process.
7 .  The Members who have cast their vote prior to the 
meeting by remote e-voting may also attend the AGM 
but shall not be entitled to vote again. Once a vote is 
cast by a member, he / she shall not be allowed to alter 
it subsequently. In case a Member casts his / her vote, 
both by Remote e-Voting and e-voting at the AGM mode, 
then the voting done by Remote e-Voting shall prevail 
and the e-voting at the AGM shall be invalid.
8.  Pursuant to the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, 
a Member, entitled to attend and vote at the AGM, is 
entitled to appoint a proxy to attend and vote on his/
her behalf and the proxy need not be a Member of the 
Company. Since this AGM is being held through VC, 
physical attendance of Members has been dispensed 
with. Accordingly, the facility for appointment of proxies 
by the Members will not be available for the AGM and 
hence the Proxy Form, Attendance Slip and Route Map 
are not annexed to this Notice.
9.  The Members attending the meeting through VC/
OAVM shall be counted for the purpose of reckoning 
the quorum of the meeting under Section 103 of the Act.
10.  The Company has appointed Aashish K. Bhatt & 
Associates, Practicing Company Secretaries, as the 
Scrutinizer to scrutinize the e-voting process in a fair 
and transparent manner. The Scrutinizer will submit his 
report after completion of the scrutiny to the Chairman

PROCEDURE FOR E-VOTING
I.  Instructions for Members for Remote e-voting through 
electronic means:
 i.  In terms of the provisions of section 108 of the Act, 
read with rule 20 of the Companies (Management

We view infrastructure as a dynamic platform for 
value creation. Our business model is anchored in the belief that sustained growth is created when assets are continuously optimised, capital is deployed efficiently and value is unlocked across the infrastructure lifecycle.
“Assets in Motion. Value in Rotation. Growth 
in Redeployment.” reflects the essence of our integrated approach to building, operating, monetising and reinvesting in transport infrastructure. Guided by our proven B.E.S.T. philosophy of Bid, Execute, Stabilise and Transfer, we create high-quality assets, enhance operational performance, monetise mature projects through innovative investment structures and redeploy capital into new growth opportunities.
The highway stretching towards the horizon 
symbolises continuity, connectivity and progress. It reflects the strength of our core business, our ability to manage assets across their lifecycle 
Scan below to download this report or to read it onlineand our commitment to supporting India’s long-term infrastructure ambitions. The evolving skyline represents future opportunities shaped by disciplined capital allocation, strategic asset management and continuous innovation.
Value rotation is central to our growth engine. 
Through the transfer of stabilised assets into InvIT platforms, we unlock capital, strengthen financial flexibility and create capacity for future investments, while maintaining operational excellence. This disciplined approach enables us to maximise returns, optimise resource utilisation and sustain a resilient growth trajectory.
Beyond financial outcomes, our asset rotation 
model creates value across all capitals. It strengthens manufactured capital through world-class infrastructure, enhances intellectual capital through operational expertise and technology adoption, develops human capital through specialised capabilities, contributes to social and relationship capital by improving connectivity and economic inclusion, and supports natural capital through responsible resource management and sustainability integration.
As India advances towards becoming a globally 
competitive infrastructure economy, we remain committed to keeping assets in motion, value in rotation and growth in progression. Through disciplined execution, strategic redeployment and a focus on long-term value creation, we continue to build infrastructure that connects destinations and creates enduring value for stakeholders and generations to come.

Understanding our Integrated Reporting Approach
This Integrated Report reflects our commitment to transparent, balanced and integrated communication with stakeholders. Prepared in alignment with the International Integrated Reporting Framework, the Report explains how we create value through our strategy, governance, business model, performance and outlook across the short, medium and long term.
As one of India’s leading transport infrastructure developers, 
we operate at the intersection of economic development, connectivity and sustainable infrastructure. Our integrated reporting approach reflects how value is created through the dynamic management, optimisation and redeployment of infrastructure assets across their lifecycle. Through integrated thinking and disciplined capital allocation, we seek to create enduring value for all stakeholders while supporting India’s infrastructure development aspirations.

The Report also reflects our commitment to integrated

India’s Leading Roads and

Our EthosIRB at a Glance
IRB Infrastructure Developers Ltd. is India’s first integrated multi-national transport 
infrastructure developer in the roads and highways segment. We have built a marquee portfolio of landmark projects, including the Mumbai-Pune Expressway, Ahmedabad-Vadodara Expressway and Hyderabad Outer Ring Road.
Purpose
The purpose for our existence is to express and 
demonstrate our sincere and whole-hearted commitment towards our Society and the Nation, through the creation of World-Class Roads & Highways Infrastructure, with minimum impact to the nature and recycling of product to maximum extent, which will facilitate creation of a strong sense of belongingness among people and bring them closer through quicker connectivity that we establish to boost trade and businesses, entrepreneurships, job opportunities; socio-cultural developments to help economy grow and enhance stakeholders’ value through profitability and goodwill.Mission  
To create the comprehensive network of world-class roads and highways infrastructure in India that will bring cities and citizens closer, share and exchange values to ensure socio-economic and cultural development of the Nation.
To strengthen and grow to the leadership position 
by ensuring continual improvements in operational efficiencies, quality and services.Values  
India’s FirstEach and every one of us at IRB strives to fulfil developmental aspirations of the Nation.
Quality, Reliability & Safety
We make sure that our infrastructure projects are of the supreme quality, highly reliable and safe for users.
Morality & Ethics
Our conduct and actions will at all times be moral and ethical. We would never resort to any action or work or involve in such an act, which are illegal, immoral and/or unethical.
Ownership & Stability
Each one of us at IRB is committed to function with high responsibility, like a stakeholder, so as to ensure growth, stability and sense of security for the organisation.

Chairman and MD’s Message
Dear Stakeholders,
Twenty-eight years ago, IRB set out with a single ambition: to build and 
operate world-class road infrastructure for India. FY 2025-26 is the year that ambition came of age. If I were to describe it in one word, it would be Transformative – not as a description of a single good year, but as the culmination of a strategy conceived, tested and refined over two and a half decades.
Our B.E.S.T. strategy – Bid, Execute, Stabilise and Transfer 
– is not a slogan we adopted this year; it is the distilled wisdom acquired through years of building, owning and operating highways across India. In FY 2025-26, that wisdom translated into decisive, tangible value creation and firmly established IRB as India’s foremost disciplined capital-recycling infrastructure platform – a position we set out deliberately to earn, and one that is now genuinely difficult to replicate.
It is a matter of real satisfaction that this disciplined 
approach has built one of India’s leading, and the largest, highway infrastructure asset platforms. Today, the IRB Group commands an asset base of approximately `94,000 Cr , up from around ` 80,000 Cr  at the start of the 
year. We operate 28 highway assets across 13 states , 
serving millions of road users every day, with our network generating over ` 1 Cr in toll revenue every hour . This did 
not happen by chance – it is the compounding result of a platform built asset by asset, cycle by cycle, and it reflects the resilience, quality and maturity of a portfolio that stands without a true peer in the Indian roads sector.
Yet the true measure of our success extends well beyond 
the numbers. Somewhere on a national highway in India at this very moment, a truck is moving seamlessly through a toll plaza we developed, a family is travelling on a road we operate and maintain, and another digital toll transaction is being processed across our network. These everyday moments, repeated millions of times, are the quiet but powerful proof of the role our infrastructure plays in connecting India, facilitating commerce and supporting the nation’s economic growth – and they are, for IRB, the most meaningful validation of everything this platform was built to do.
Our B.E.S.T. 
strategy remains the cornerstone of our value-creation philosophy, and FY 2025-26 was the year it truly proved itself as a capability that sets IRB apart.India continues to be one of the world’s fastest-growing 
major economies. Despite geopolitical uncertainties and global economic volatility, the resilience of the Indian economy continued to drive growth in both passenger mobility and freight movement, reflected in healthy traffic growth across our portfolio and stronger toll collections, particularly in the second half of the year. This performance is an affirmation – of the quality of our assets, the resilience of our business model, and the conviction with which we have built for India’s long-term infrastructure story.
FY 2025-26 marked another year of strong operational 
execution across our tolling portfolio. Our highways today serve nearly 1.5 Mn vehicles every day and account for close to 10% of India’s total toll collections . Toll revenue 
across IRB and our Private InvIT platform grew by nearly 13% year-on-year , driven by healthy traffic growth, periodic 
tariff revisions and the addition of new operational assets.
All major projects are now operational. The capex cycle 
is complete. We enter the next phase from a position of strength, with future growth driven by operating leverage, rising toll collections, InvIT distributions, asset rotation and recurring O&M income.
From Builder to Owner-Operator: A Strategic Coming 
of Age
FY 2025-26 was a defining year – the year our strategic 
transformation was truly completed. Over its operating life, IRB consciously and deliberately reshaped its identity from a contractor: first into a developer that took on construction risk and ownership, and now into a Sponsor and Operations & Maintenance-led platform, with a sharp focus on capital efficiency, recurring cash flows, long-term annuity income and sustainable shareholder returns. Few infrastructure companies in India have made this full journey – from contractor, to developer, to institutional owner-operator – and fewer still have done so while continuing to grow the underlying portfolio at the pace we have.
This is more than a change in business mix. It is the 
evolution of IRB from a project development company into a platform built on creating, owning, operating and monetising high-quality road infrastructure assets at scale.  It strengthens the resilience of our business model, 
sharpens earnings visibility, and positions us to deliver consistent, compounding value for every stakeholder who has placed their trust in us.
B.E.S.T.: The Engine Behind an Incomparable 
Platform
Our B.E.S.T. strategy remains the cornerstone of our 
value-creation philosophy, and FY 2025-26 was the year it truly proved itself as a capability that sets IRB apart. This continuous, disciplined rotation of assets – bidding, executing, stabilising and transferring — is the engine behind our growth: every rupee of equity is made to work multiple times over, rather than being committed once and held for decades. It is this capital velocity, built and refined over years of execution, that has allowed us to construct a portfolio whose scale and quality are, today, genuinely difficult for others to match.

and reaffirming the discipline behind every transfer we execute.
As we continue to execute this capital allocation and 
value-creation strategy with conviction, we are steadily reducing the Company’s consolidated net debt, with a clear objective of achieving a net debt-free position over the next five years.  This deleveraging trajectory will enhance 
our financial resilience, improve cash return on equity, and give us the flexibility to pursue the next phase of growth from a position of genuine strength.
A Portfolio that Stands Apart
Although overall project award activity remained relatively subdued during the year, IRB Infrastructure Trust continued to strengthen its portfolio by securing TOT-17 and TOT-18 , 
with an aggregate enterprise value of approximately `14,000 Cr  – well above our typical annual project 
additions. Once again, we demonstrated the execution excellence that has become our hallmark: achieving financial closure for TOT-17 within a remarkably short span, and successfully commencing tolling operations on TOT-17 and TOT-18 on January 23, 2026 and April 1, 2026, respectively . Collections from both assets have been in line 
with our expectations since commencement, reaffirming our confidence in their long-term potential. TOT-17 carries, for IRB, a particular significance – connecting some of India’s most revered pilgrimage and heritage destinations, and enabling safer, faster and more efficient travel for millions of commuters and devotees.
With every project across our platform now operational, 
IRB has entered a new phase – one defined by earnings stability, operating leverage and long-term revenue visibility that few of our peers can claim. The resilience of our business model rests on a portfolio in which over 99% of our assets are fully constructed and operational, toll tariffs are contractually linked to inflation, and operations and maintenance costs account for only around 15% of our total cost base. These structural advantages give us predictable cash flows, resilience across economic cycles, and a portfolio quality that clearly and durably differentiates IRB from conventional construction-led infrastructure companies.
O&M: The Rising Pillar
Our Operations & Maintenance platform is emerging as one of the strongest pillars of our future earnings visibility. Unlike conventional EPC-led models that depend on continuous order-book replenishment, our O&M business provides long-duration, annuity-style revenues with stable margins and predictable cash flows. Our O&M order book alone stands at ` 428 Bn, offering 15 to 20 years of 
long-term visibility with healthy margins. We expect the contribution of O&M revenues to keep increasing steadily, further improving the quality, stability and sustainability of our earnings profile.
ESG, Governance, and Our Communities
At IRB, sustainability is not a statement – it is a practice embedded in every aspect of our operations. Our investments in renewable energy solutions, reuse of Reclaimed Asphalt Product, eco-engineering techniques and low-carbon construction practices underscore this commitment, and IRB is rated among the top infrastructure companies in India for ESG performance.
Our long-term CSR programmes focus on health, 
education, water conservation and community empowerment. Initiatives such as the Sujalam Sufalam Schemes reflect our commitment to putting our resources to work for social good. We continue to maintain robust governance through independent boards, comprehensive grievance mechanisms, and ISO certifications across quality, environment and occupational health (9001, 14001 and 45001).
Pioneering Digital, and Now AI
Innovation has always been integral to IRB’s growth journey. We have consistently embraced technology not merely to improve efficiency, but to change the way highway infrastructure is developed, operated and managed. Over the years, IRB has stayed at the forefront of digital adoption in the Indian roads sector – we were among the pioneers of one of India’s first pilot projects for FASTag-based electronic toll collection, and among the first infrastructure companies to implement an integrated SAP enterprise platform, seamlessly connected with our Toll Management System, enabling real-time financial and operational reporting across our portfolio.Today, more than 97% of our toll revenue is collected digitally through FASTag , with transactions recorded 
automatically and with no human intervention – enhancing operational efficiency, improving transparency, strengthening internal controls and delivering a superior experience for highway users.
Artificial Intelligence now represents the next frontier of 
this journey. IRB is pleased to share that it has initiated the implementation of AI-driven solutions across its Operations and Maintenance activities, aimed at enhancing preventive maintenance, improving asset monitoring, strengthening safety management and enabling more data-driven decision-making. While these initiatives are still being rolled out, AI, together with advanced analytics and digital technologies, is expected to further improve operational excellence, enhance customer experience and support more efficient lifecycle management of our highway assets – adopted, as always, thoughtfully and responsibly, in a manner that creates sustainable value for our stakeholders.
Our philosophy remains unchanged: technology is not an 
end in itself – it is an enabler of safer roads, better customer service, more efficient operations and stronger long-term value creation.
Other Updates
In line with the Company’s Dividend Distribution Policy, we declared total dividends of approximately ` 187 Cr during 
FY 2025-26.
During the year, the Company also received distributions 
of approximately ` 300 Cr from its two InvIT platforms – a 
clear reflection of the robust and steadily improving cash-generating ability of our mature operational assets as they continue to stabilise and grow.
The Company also completed a 1:1 bonus Issue announced 
during the year, reaffirming our confidence in IRB’s long-term growth prospects.The Road Ahead
Following the transfer of three BOT assets from IRB Infrastructure Trust and one HAM asset from IRB Infra, the Private InvIT has proposed the sale of two BOT highway assets, with an enterprise value of approximately ` 4,605 Cr , 
to the Public InvIT – the B.E.S.T. strategy continuing to do exactly what it was built to do. The capital unlocked will be redeployed into our next phase of growth.
Building on this momentum, we remain firmly on track to 
expand our road asset portfolio to nearly ` 1.4 trillion  over 
the next three to four years – a target that reflects just how far this platform has travelled since IRB’s earliest days as a road-building company.
Toll-Operate-Transfer (TOT) projects will continue to be 
our primary growth driver. With the Government’s road monetisation pipeline estimated at approximately ` 4.4 
trillion  over the next four to five years – representing 
annual TOT opportunities of ` 400–500 Bn  – IRB is well 
positioned to capitalise on this sizeable opportunity through the very capabilities that define us: an integrated platform, disciplined capital allocation, and proven expertise in acquiring, operating and monetising toll-road assets at a scale few in this industry can match.
Gratitude
On behalf of the Board, I extend my sincere appreciation to our shareholders for their continued trust and confidence – trust that has made this journey from builder to owner-operator possible. I also thank the National Highways Authority of India, MSRDC, HMDA, UPEIDA, our lending institutions, investors, business partners and government authorities for their continued support and collaboration.
Most importantly, I express my heartfelt gratitude to every 
member of the IRB family. Their commitment, integrity and relentless pursuit of excellence have built, brick by brick and highway by highway, the platform we stand on today.
As we look ahead, we remain committed to creating 
sustainable long-term value through disciplined capital allocation, operational excellence, prudent risk management and the highest standards of corporate governance. These principles will continue to guide IRB as we build infrastructure that contributes to India’s growth, while delivering enduring value for our shareholders. 
Warm regards,
Virendra D. MhaiskarChairman & Managing Director

We maintain structured engagement with our diverse 
stakeholder base, recognising that informed dialogue is essential to sound decision-making, operational continuity and sustainable value creation. Regular interactions and feedback mechanisms help us refine priorities, allocate capital effectively and direct resources towards areas of strategic, operational and societal relevance. Periodic materiality assessments further support this process by integrating evolving stakeholder expectations into corporate strategy, risk management and performance monitoring.
Accountability to stakeholders is embedded in 
our governance philosophy. We cultivate these relationships through a clearly-defined engagement architecture that reflects each stakeholder’s influence, dependency and connection to the business. This framework supports differentiated engagement across stakeholder groups, strategic partners and external influencers, ensuring that our interactions remain relevant, inclusive and responsive to changing business conditions, regulatory developments and project-level realities.

Priorities that Guide our AscentMateriality Assessment
A robust materiality assessment guides how we focus our sustainability efforts and report 
transparently on the issues that matter most to stakeholders and long-term value creation. Building on previous assessments, we strengthened our approach in FY 2025-26 to reflect both our most significant impacts and the ESG issues that are financially material to the business.
Grounded in GRI 3 and informed by leading ESG 
rating methodologies, SASB, IFRS S1/S2 and SEBI’s BRSR framework, our double materiality approach evaluates environmental, social and governance topics through three lenses: stakeholder concerns, impact on enterprise value and impact on the broader economy, environment and society. This helps us connect stakeholder engagement, risk management and strategy, while ensuring that our disclosures reflect the ESG factors shaping our future performance.Methodology Evolution and Standards 
Alignment
During FY 2025-26, we further evolved materiality 
from a compliance-led exercise into a strategic tool that guides how we allocate time, capital and management attention. Our enhanced double materiality assessment elevated occupational health and safety, climate resilience, governance and ethics, human capital and responsible supply chains as key issues for stakeholders and future performance.
We continued our practice of peer benchmarking and sectoral assessment using the SASB Engineering & Construction Services Standard. We also aligned the process with GRI 3 Material Topics 2021, GRI Universal Standards 2021, IFRS S1/S2 guidance and SEBI’s BRSR framework. These references ensure that our topic universe reflects both impact materiality under GRI and financial materiality as viewed by investors and rating agencies.
The key advancement in our methodology is the integration 
of impacts, risks and opportunities into a dynamic double materiality framework. Each topic is assessed across three dimensions:
 Stakeholder concerns
 Impact on the organisation, covering enterprise value
 Impact on sustainability, covering the economy, environment and people
A topic is considered material when it has significant actual or potential impacts on people or the environment, or when it could reasonably influence the decisions of investors and other providers of capital due to its effect on enterprise value. Our matrix brings these perspectives together and positions each topic based on its importance to stakeholders and to the business.External Frameworks, ESG Rating Methodologies 
and Peer Benchmarking
To complement the GRI 3 impact lens, we mapped 
our topic universe to leading ESG rating providers and sector frameworks.
 ESG Rating Methodologies
We reviewed construction and infrastructure sector 
priorities identified by leading ESG rating providers. These include health and safety, human capital development, labour management, community relations, opportunities in clean technology and water, board effectiveness, ownership and control, accounting, business ethics and tax transparency. This helped confirm the prominence of governance, safety and workforce-related topics in our matrix.
 Materiality Maps and Industry Drivers
Sector materiality maps and industry driver analysis 
emphasise strong corporate governance and ethical standards, climate transition and physical risk management, sustainable raw materials, waste management and advanced human capital management in a labour-intensive sector. These references provided a useful cross-check for our double materiality positioning by assessing both external impact on society and the environment and impact on enterprise value creation.

 SASB Engineering & Construction Services Standard
SASB guidance was used to ensure coverage of sector-
relevant financially material topics, including climate and environmental management, project and construction safety, human capital, supply chain practices, data security and business ethics.
 Peer Benchmarking
We conducted structured benchmarking against leading 
national peers and one international infrastructure and construction peer to confirm sector relevance, identify emerging themes and calibrate the long list of topics. Insights from peer materiality matrices reinforced the importance of occupational health and safety, climate and resource efficiency, human capital, governance and ethics, responsible supply chains, community relations and data security.
GRI 3 Impact Lens
In line with GRI 3, each potential material topic was assessed for positive and negative impacts, with particular attention to human rights implications. Negative impacts were further categorised as:
 Caused by the Organisation
Impacts arising directly from our own activities, such 
as safety conditions at construction sites or emissions from equipment.
 Contributed by the Organisation
Impacts where we are not the sole cause, but where 
our decisions or practices influence outcomes, such as project timelines or cost structures that may pressure contractors’ safety or labour practices.
 Directly Linked to the Organisation
Impacts caused by value chain partners but linked to us 
through business relationships, such as subcontractor labour practices or raw material sourcing impacts.
This analysis supports clearer allocation of responsibility and more targeted response strategies, ranging from direct remediation where we cause impacts to leverage-based engagement across the value chain.
Stakeholder Engagement and Materiality Analysis
Our materiality assessment is closely linked to our stakeholder engagement framework. Internal respondents representing key stakeholder groups, including investors and shareholders, government and authorities, employees, suppliers and subcontractors, customers and clients, and local communities, participated in the annual materiality survey and workshops.Materiality Matrix and FY 2025-26 Validation
The outcome of this process is a double materiality matrix in which each issue is positioned based on its impact on stakeholders on the y-axis and its impact on enterprise value on the x-axis. The matrix provides a strategic overview of our sustainability priorities and highlights the issues that require focused management, resource allocation and enhanced disclosure.
The matrix is reviewed annually. For FY 2025-26, previously 
identified material topics were reassessed and validated using the enhanced approach, incorporating updated stakeholder feedback, ERM insights, GRI 3 impact categorisation and external references from ESG rating providers and peer benchmarking. This exercise confirmed the continued relevance of our existing topics, while refining their prioritisation and strengthening their linkage to strategy and risk management.Inputs were analysed across three questions:
 Stakeholder Concerns
What issues matter most to our stakeholders?
 Impact on the OrganisationHow do these issues influence business operations, 
reputation and financial performance?
 Impact on Sustainability
What are the environmental and social implications 
associated with these issues?
The resulting scores feed into the double materiality matrix, with stakeholder concern forming one axis of prioritisation alongside impact on enterprise value. Our stakeholder saliency framework, covering power, legitimacy, urgency and vulnerability, also guides whose inputs carry greater weight for specific topics. For example, community inputs are especially relevant to road safety and access issues, while investor and regulator inputs are critical to governance and ethics.
Through this analysis, 13 material issues critical to our 
strategic focus were identified and validated by the ESG Committee to ensure alignment with our sustainability goals, risk appetite and stakeholder expectations.
Scoring Methodology and ERM Integration
We have integrated our Enterprise Risk Management process into the materiality framework to strengthen the robustness of our assessment. This enables us to systematically identify and evaluate risk factors, emerging trends, impact severity and likelihood of occurrence. It also supports targeted ESG strategies and provides deeper insight into sustainability impacts as both risks and opportunities.
Prioritisation of material issues is guided by a structured 
scoring methodology that combines stakeholder feedback with risk assessment. For each topic, we consider:
 Scale
Severity of the impact.
 ScopeExtent of affected people, assets or geographies.
 Irremediable CharacterDifficulty of reversing or mitigating harm, especially for 
negative impacts.
 Likelihood
Probability of occurrence.
These criteria are applied across impacts, risks and 
opportunities, and then integrated with our ERM framework to align topic scoring with risk registers, emerging risk monitoring and capital allocation decisions. This ensures that ESG topics with high risk or opportunity implications receive appropriate governance and management attention.Materiality Matrix
The materiality matrix presents the relative positioning of key ESG topics identified through internal stakeholder surveys, risk analysis and alignment with global reporting frameworks. These prioritised issues form the foundation of our ESG strategy and risk management approach. Strengthening Resilience through 
Strategic Risk ManagementRisk Management
We understand the importance of addressing risks proactively to safeguard our 
stakeholders’ interests and ensure long-term sustainability.  To achieve this, we have established a robust risk management mechanism that systematically identifies, assesses, monitors and mitigates risks that could potentially impact our operations. We believe that by taking a proactive approach to risk management, we can effectively mitigate potential threats and capitalise on opportunities that align with our strategic objectives.
Our risk management framework encompasses risks 
arising from the environmental, social and governance perspective. This approach allows us to consider risk events related to climate change, social responsibility and governance practices and develop mitigation strategies for such events.
Risk Governance
The Board constituted a Risk Management Committee that oversees the implementation of the risk management policy, including evaluating the adequacy of risk management systems.The Committee is updated semi-annually on the potential risks, including climate-related risks and relevant mitigation measures for the same. The Committee also provides guidance for enhancing the Company’s resilience.
The Company has in place dedicated teams at the 
Function-level and Site-level to ensure that the relevant mitigation measures are implemented in real time and at all levels. Moreover, periodic business function & project reviews are conducted to ensure that timely actions are taken for identified risks. These also include discussions on risks specific to each function or project, including climate-related risks.

The Risk Management Committee is briefed on the status of mitigation measures regularly and if significant breakdowns in risk controls are observed, the Committee instructs risk owners for corrective action.
The risk management process at IRB enhances 
the organisation’s ability to prevent or mitigate potential negative impacts after due consideration of any associated potential opportunity. It allows for proactive decision-making, resource allocation and the establishment of robust control mechanisms. The Company fosters a strong culture to take informed decisions while carefully evaluating the impact of risks in protecting its assets, reputation and overall objectives.
Framework to Determine Risk Appetite
Overview: To enhance our enterprise risk management process, IRB has conducted systematically identifying, assessing, and mitigating risks, utilising COSO ERM 2017 in its enterprise risk policy. The COSO Enterprise Risks Management Process fosters transparency and ethics of conducting business in the manner of alignment with international practices, allowing IRB to conduct effective decision-making and resilience against external business risks.
Risk Appetite: Under the governance of board 
constituted Risk Management Committee (RMC) as per prescribed terms of reference set by SEBI, IRB has established risk appetite statement, in accordance with the guidance of COSO ERM 2017, to define the level of risk the company is willing to accept. The risk appetite will provide threshold, as the acceptable level, covered all the identified risks. The Risk Management Committee (RMC) is responsible of setting the overall risk appetite for the organisation and ensure the alignment with the company's strategic objectives and risk capacity. Meanwhile, the responsibility of Risk Management Committee (RMC) includes ensuring that the implementation of risk management is aligned with strategic management, linked to strategic objectives and primary goals of the organisation, within risk appetite and in conformity to policy and risk management framework established. Risk Culture and Training
IRB’s risk culture is based on the principles of openness, transparency, accountability, ethics, empowering risk owners to take informed decisions and continual improvement. This is achieved by setting the tone at the top, imparting comprehensive training, conducting awareness sessions across corporate functions.
The leadership ensures that business objectives, 
policies and the importance of risk management are clearly articulated throughout the organisation.
The risk management training encompasses 
understanding the Company’s risk management policy, creation of risk registers, risk assessment and evaluation, mitigation measures and understanding of best practices of risk management as per globally renowned risk management frameworks.
Each department is responsible for identifying and 
managing risks specific to their area of expertise. The Company has also employed dedicated teams responsible for assessing and mitigating risks associated with each project. Regular risk assessments and proactive risk mitigation strategies are integrated into bidding, project planning and execution.
This approach encourages employees to not only 
identify and report risks but also to take ownership of these risks, creating a culture of shared responsibility and accountability. This practice helps the Company in developing a robust risk management culture.
Risk Management Process
Risk events are systematically identified, assessed and prioritised based on their likelihood of occurrence and potential impact on established objectives. Following the identification of risks, a thorough description is provided and identified risks are assessed based on the Risk Evaluation Framework to estimate their potential impact and likelihood of occurrence. Specific control measures are evaluated to mitigate each of the risks. The combination of the potential impact of a risk and its likelihood is used to determine its intensity and scores are calculated to carry out analysis. We conduct a comprehensive analysis semi-annually, supplemented by selective reviews every quarter, ensuring a robust and adaptive assessment process. Using this process and in alignment with SEBI LODR, IRB’s ERM framework addresses risks under 5 categories of risks.

India’s transition from WPI to Producer Price Index (PPI)
Context
The IRB’s annual horizon scanning exercise identified 
distinct developments in India’s price index framework that create unprecedented uncertainty for infrastructure concessions whose revenue streams are indexed to wholesale price benchmarks. This exercise is supported by analysis of regulatory publications from NHAI, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry (DPIIT), and MoSPI. These developments were reviewed by the IRB’s Finance and Risk functions in and formally elevated to the emerging risk register on the basis that they represent a structural change to the indexation architecture of infrastructure concession agreements – a change arising from a reconciliation of the linking factor with data published by the Office of the Economic Adviser and couldn’t have been anticipated when the older concession agreements were finalised.
Price index linkage and the risk of indexation 
underperformance relative to actual cost inflation have long been features of India’s infrastructure concession landscape. What elevates the current situation to an emerging risk of a different and unprecedented character is due to recent and specific development as mentioned below.
Recently, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry released 
India’s inaugural Producer Price Index data, marking the commencement of a formally announced transition from WPI – the benchmark embedded in all major NHAI concession agreements for annual toll rate revision – to PPI over a five-year horizon. The WPI will be progressively discontinued by 2031. The PPI, while methodologically superior in its measurement of producer-level price dynamics and aligned with international standards including IMF recommendations, differs structurally from WPI in its basket composition, stage-of-production measurement, and treatment of services. The trajectory of PPI relative to WPI across commodity cycles is not yet established given the absence of a PPI historical time series under the new 2022-23 base. The Company notes that existing concession agreements reference WPI specifically, and the contractual and regulatory pathway for rebasing toll indexation to PPI is ultimately a policy question for NHAI and MoRTH. This introduces an unprecedented period of indexation uncertainty that the Company is actively monitoring. Mitigation
 Constructive regulatory engagement  
The Company actively participates in industry 
forums, including representations through relevant associations and direct engagement with NHAI and MoRTH, to contribute to the development of practical and equitable frameworks for the WPI-to-PPI transition in concession agreement contexts. The Company believes that the government’s commitment to a consultative approach to major policy transitions provides an appropriate pathway for industry concerns to be addressed constructively.
 Concession agreement gap analysis  
The Company notes that it approaches this matter as a constructive stakeholder in India’s infrastructure development ecosystem and is confident that the government and NHAI, through their established frameworks for concessionaire engagement, will develop an equitable and operationally practical resolution to the indexation transition. A review of all active concession and project agreements informs the Company’s legal preparedness without prejudging any outcome. Potential Business Impact
 Indexation rebasing creates uncertainty on toll rates:  For the Company’s BOT and HAM concession 
assets whose toll revision formula references WPI, the transition to PPI creates a period uncertainty during which the annual escalation is applicable to toll rates.
 Concession agreement gap: The model concession agreements doesn’t contain provisions specifically governing the scenario of the referenced WPI series being discontinued and replaced by an alternative index. This creates a contractual gap that will need 
to be addressed – through regulatory guidance, concession agreement amendments, circular or any 
other suitable mechanism.

Governance
At IRB, climate-related governance is integrated at the 
highest levels of decision-making. The Board-level Risk Management Committee (RMC) holds strategic oversight on environmental and climate-related risks and opportunities. The Committee routinely assesses IRB’s exposure to climate impacts, evolving regulatory landscapes, and progress against sustainability targets.
As part of IRB’s enterprise-wide risk review and business 
continuity planning, climate change considerations are formally embedded. Projects with potential vulnerability to climate risks undergo rigorous assessment and engineering interventions in accordance with Relevant Authority’s procedures & guidelines. This includes climate-resilient project design and its execution under the supervision of an Independent Engineer appointed by Authority and Authority’s officials. The executed projects are operationalised after obtaining due clearances from Authority, ensuring robust internal controls.
This governance approach enables IRB to proactively 
address climate-related risks while capitalising on low-carbon transition opportunities, particularly in areas such as energy efficiency, and sustainable infrastructure development.
Strategy
IRB has defined its short-term (0–5 years), medium-term (5–10 years), and long-term (Beyond 10 years) strategy after a comprehensive peer benchmarking exercise. These time frames form the basis for assessing the materiality of climate-related risks and opportunities and are embedded into risk reviews, strategic planning, and investment decision frameworks.
Based on the IPCC RCP Scenarios and seven NGFS climate 
scenarios, IRB has proactively identified a spectrum of transition risks, physical risks, and emerging opportunities across its diversified portfolio of businesses-ranging from BOT and TOT to HAM and airport operations. These insights help shape IRB’s medium- and long-term resilience strategy under the framework of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD).
For identifying and assessing physical risks, IRB has 
considered IPCC’s Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP), RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5. For transition risks, IRB utilised India’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), Below 2°C Scenario, NGFS Current Policy and Net Zero 2050 Scenarios. We mapped the plausible business impact of the following categories of risks and opportunities:
Physical Risks
Physical risks are a result of short-term catastrophes (acute) 
or long-term variations in climate patterns (chronic). Acute physical risks are those that are triggered by a specific event, such as extreme weather events like cyclones, storms or floods. Whereas longer-term changes in climatic patterns (e.g. prolonged higher temperatures) may produce sea level rise or chronic heat waves, which are referred to as chronic physical hazards.
Transition Risks
Transition risks are enterprise risks that arise as a result of 
societal and economic transformations toward a low carbon, more environmentally friendly future. These risks can include policy and regulatory and legal risks, technological risks, market risks and reputational risks. These areas can vary in terms of their type, focus and geographical acceptance, which can have a financial implication on our business.

IRB integrates climate-related risks into its enterprise

Climate risks are identified and assessed across physical and transition categories, drawing on inputs from site-level qualitative assessments under IPCC RCPs and NGFS pathways, and stakeholder consultations. The risks are evaluated for materiality based on their likelihood, business unit vulnerability, and potential financial impact, and are prioritised using a composite scoring model. 
These climate risks are reviewed periodically by 
the Risk Management Committee and incorporated into the corporate risk register alongside traditional operational, financial, and regulatory risks. Mitigation measures – ranging from capital expenditure decisions to adaptation strategies – are integrated into business planning cycles. This process ensures that climate risk is not treated as a standalone issue but is embedded into the Company’s governance, planning, and performance evaluation mechanisms.
This framework is tailored to consider objectives pertaining 
to operations, reporting, and compliance. Leveraging this, IRB systematically evaluates risks and opportunities at both the asset/plant and corporate levels. The mitigation plans and advancements toward achieving low-carbon and sustainable development targets undergo thorough review and approval by the ESG Committee and RMC and inform business continuity planning, site-level investments, and the Company’s broader climate strategy. This integrated approach ensures climate risk is managed alongside conventional operational, regulatory, and financial risks, as part of a unified Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework.Metrics and Targets
IRB monitors and discloses climate-related performance using a robust set of quantitative and qualitative metrics aligned with its business model, sectoral context, and stakeholder expectations. These metrics are used to track progress on mitigation, adaptation, and climate resilience initiatives, as well as inform decision-making at the Board and management levels.
Key metrics tracked include:
 GHG Emissions : Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions 
reporting is fully aligned with BRSR and Industry 
Standards Forum (ISF) requirements. In FY 2025-26, the Company assessed and reported emissions across four identified Scope 3 categories
 Emission Intensity : Sector-specific intensity metrics 
are used
 Water Management : Water withdrawal, discharge, and 
recharge data is monitored at all sites. Under the Sujalam Sufalam Scheme, we undertook water conservation and management initiatives benefiting local communities. This project created 53,427 cubic metres of water bodies, serving two villages with a combined population of around 4,700+ residents
 Renewable Energy Usage : Metrics on RE share in total

Enabling Trust, Governance and Resilient Digital 
Infrastructure
As one of India's leading transport infrastructure developers 
and operators, IRB recognises information security, cybersecurity and digital resilience as critical enablers of operational reliability, stakeholder trust and long-term value creation. The Company's extensive network of toll plazas, FASTag-enabled infrastructure, traffic management systems, project offices and enterprise applications requires a robust approach to safeguarding information assets and ensuring continuity of critical operations.
Information security forms an integral part of IRB's 
governance and risk management framework. The Company's Information Security Management System (ISMS), certified to ISO 27001:2022, provides a structured and internationally recognised framework for identifying, assessing, monitoring and mitigating information security risks across its operations. Through this framework, IRB seeks to protect information assets, strengthen cyber resilience, support regulatory compliance and enable secure digital transformation across its business.
Recognising the increasing digitalisation of infrastructure 
operations and the evolving cybersecurity threat landscape, the Company continues to strengthen its security capabilities through risk-based governance, technology controls, employee awareness and continuous improvement mechanisms. These efforts support the protection of operational systems, business information and stakeholder data while reinforcing resilience against cyber threats and operational disruptions.
Governance & Oversight
IRB's information security framework operates through 
defined governance mechanisms embedded within its enterprise risk management structure. Cybersecurity and information security risks are periodically assessed and monitored as part of the Company's broader risk management processes, ensuring alignment with strategic priorities, operational requirements and stakeholder expectations.
The ISO 27001-certified Information Security Management 
System establishes clear responsibilities, policies, procedures and accountability mechanisms for managing information security risks across the organisation. Information security governance is supported through periodic management reviews, internal audits, surveillance assessments and continuous monitoring activities designed to ensure the ongoing effectiveness of controls and risk mitigation measures.
This governance approach is complemented by a 
structured lines-of-defence model, under which business and operational functions manage day-to-day risks, information security teams provide specialist oversight and guidance, and independent assurance activities evaluate the effectiveness of controls and compliance with established requirements.Information Security Risk Management
IRB follows a structured risk-based approach to information 
security in accordance with the requirements of ISO 27001:2022. Risks relating to cyber threats, data protection, tolling systems, operational technologies, third-party access, cloud environments and business continuity are identified, assessed and evaluated through defined risk management processes.
Risk treatment plans are developed and monitored based 
on the significance of identified risks and the effectiveness of existing controls. Information security risks are integrated within the broader Enterprise Risk Management framework, enabling management to proactively address emerging threats while strengthening operational resilience across the organisation.
Security Framework & Controls
IRB's cybersecurity architecture is built on a layered 
defence approach designed to safeguard corporate systems, tolling infrastructure, operational technologies and critical business applications. The framework incorporates network security controls, endpoint protection, identity and access management, secure system configurations, vulnerability management, threat monitoring and incident response capabilities.
Particular emphasis is placed on protecting critical 
infrastructure supporting toll collection operations, FASTag-enabled systems, traffic management platforms and associated operational technologies. Security controls are designed to safeguard system availability, data integrity and operational continuity while reducing exposure to cyber threats and unauthorised access.
The Company continuously reviews and strengthens 
its cybersecurity controls to address evolving risks across enterprise systems, digital infrastructure and operational environments.
Data Privacy & Information Protection
The Company maintains structured controls to protect 
information assets throughout their lifecycle. Information security policies, access controls, information classification requirements and secure data handling protocols support the protection of employee, customer, vendor and business-critical information.
Role-based access mechanisms ensure that information 
is accessible only to authorised personnel based on business requirements. Monitoring processes, periodic reviews and control assessments support the detection and prevention of unauthorised access, disclosure or misuse of information assets.
Privacy and information protection measures are aligned 
with applicable regulatory requirements and support the Company's commitment to safeguarding stakeholder information and maintaining trust across its operations.Third-Party Information Security
IRB recognises that information security extends beyond 
organisational boundaries and includes risks arising from technology providers, service partners, consultants and other third parties with access to systems or information assets.
Information security considerations are incorporated 
into vendor onboarding, procurement and technology engagement processes through risk-based due diligence and control assessments. These evaluations support the identification and management of potential cybersecurity risks arising from external relationships and contribute to strengthening supply chain resilience.
The Company continues to enhance third-party 
cybersecurity oversight in recognition of the increasing interconnectedness of digital ecosystems and infrastructure operations.
Cyber Risk Management
Cybersecurity risks are actively managed through a 
combination of preventive, detective and responsive controls. The Company undertakes periodic Vulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing (VAPT), security monitoring activities, control reviews and risk assessments to identify vulnerabilities and strengthen cyber resilience across its technology landscape.
Security measures are continuously enhanced to address 
emerging risks affecting digital infrastructure, enterprise applications, cloud environments and operational systems. Cybersecurity considerations are integrated into broader risk management processes to support proactive identification, mitigation and monitoring of cyber threats that may impact business continuity and operational performance.
Cyber Awareness & Human Firewall
Recognising that employees are a critical line of defence 
against cyber threats, IRB continues to strengthen its human firewall through structured awareness and capability-building initiatives.
Regular cybersecurity awareness programmes, policy 
communications and training interventions help employees understand emerging threats, cybersecurity responsibilities and secure digital practices. These initiatives support the development of a strong cybersecurity culture while reducing human-related security risks such as phishing, social engineering and unauthorised disclosure of information.
Through continuous engagement and awareness efforts, 
the Company seeks to embed responsible digital behaviour across all levels of the organisation.Cyber Incident Management
IRB has established structured processes for managing 
cybersecurity incidents and responding to emerging threats. These processes define responsibilities and protocols for incident identification, classification, escalation, investigation, reporting and recovery.
The Company's incident management framework follows a 
systematic lifecycle approach encompassing preparedness, detection, response, investigation, reporting and recovery. Insights derived from incident reviews, assessments and monitoring activities are used to strengthen controls, improve response-readiness and support continuous enhancement of cybersecurity capabilities.
Business Continuity and Cyber Resilience
Maintaining operational continuity across toll operations, 
project execution activities and corporate functions is a key priority for IRB. Business Continuity Planning (BCP) and Disaster Recovery (DR) mechanisms have been established to support resilience against cyber incidents, technology disruptions and other operational events.
These arrangements include backup protocols, recovery 
procedures, incident response strategies and resilience testing activities designed to minimise operational disruption and facilitate timely restoration of critical systems and services. Periodic testing and review of continuity arrangements help ensure preparedness and strengthen organisational resilience.
Information Security Audit and Assurance
The effectiveness of IRB's Information Security 
Management System is periodically evaluated through internal audits, management reviews, surveillance assessments and independent external evaluations. These assessments examine governance processes, risk management practices, technical controls, access management mechanisms and information protection measures.
Findings from audit and assurance activities are used to 
strengthen controls, implement corrective actions and drive continual improvement of the information security framework. This process supports ongoing alignment with ISO 27001 requirements, evolving regulatory expectations and emerging industry best practices.

Sustainability governance framework
We have instituted a structured ESG governance framework anchored in Board-level oversight and supported by a dedicated ESG Committee. The Board of Directors is accountable for material environmental, social and governance matters, including climate-related risks and opportunities discharged through the ESG Committee and other relevant Board committees, in line with applicable regulatory expectations.
The ESG Committee provides strategic direction on 
ESG priorities, recommends key policies and targets to the Board, and reviews performance against material ESG indicators and regulatory disclosures, including the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR).ESG Committee and executive leadership
Under the guidance and oversight of the Board, we have established an ESG Committee comprising senior executives responsible for driving the sustainability agenda across the organisation. The Committee is chaired by a senior management member and includes cross-functional leaders from Finance, Corporate Affairs & Company Secretarial, Human Resources & Administration, Project Monitoring and Evaluation, Health & Safety, Environment, Operations and Risk Management.
The ESG Committee meets at defined intervals, at

We leverage a networked governance model with cross-functional participation to ensure that ESG responsibilities are entrenched in business operations. Under the ESG Committee, functional heads and business unit leaders act as ESG representatives within their respective domains, supported by designated ESG single points of contact (SPOCs).

Economic Value Added
In FY 2025-26, we generated direct economic value of ` 78,540 Mn, supported by steady revenue from our BOT, TOT and 
HAM portfolios, along with income from asset monetisation platforms such as InvITs.
Our financial capital has remained resilient over the past four years, supported by disciplined capital allocation, prudent 
cost management and a sustained focus on stakeholder value. Total income in FY 2025-26 stood at ` 78,540 Mn, including 
`2,058 Mn from financial investments and other sources. Of this, ` 67,627 Mn was distributed among stakeholders, while 
`10,913 Mn was retained for reinvestment, compared with ` 7,902 Mn in the previous year. 
Performance Review
FY 2025-26 was marked by stable profitability and disciplined execution, supported by resilient cash flows, sustained margins and increasing contributions from maturing toll concessions across our private and public InvIT portfolios.
EBITDA stood at ` 41,877 Mn, with the margin remaining 
stable at 53%, reflecting cost optimisation and operating 
discipline. Profit before tax increased to ` 12,905 Mn from 
`10,573 Mn in FY 2024-25, while profit after tax rose to 
`8,931 Mn. The net profit margin was approximately 12% 
before exceptional items, net of tax, despite continued investments in project acquisitions and business expansion.
Our balanced mix of annuity and toll-based revenues 
supported profitability in a dynamic cost environment. The Debtors Turnover Ratio stood at 4.59 times, compared with 5.35 times in FY 2024-25 and 4.02 times in FY 2023-24. We continued to focus on billing efficiency, timely collections and receivables management across EPC and O&M contracts.
The Net Debt-to-Equity Ratio improved to 0.53 from 0.59 
in FY 2024-25. Short-term liabilities during the year were primarily linked to project mobilisation, toll operations and vendor payments. We continue to prioritise prudent working capital management and adequate liquidity headroom.
Earnings per share on basic and diluted basis excluding 
exceptional items to ` 0.74 for FY 2025-26 from ` 0.56 
in FY 2024-25, registering a growth of 32%. Near-term earnings are expected to be supported by strong internal accruals, while the completion and timely monetisation of large-scale assets through the InvIT platform are expected to support longer-term value creation.

Our Management System Excellence
We embed internationally recognised management systems 
across  all our project sites, toll plazas and operational hubs. Certifications under ISO 9001, ISO 14001 and ISO 45001 strengthen quality, environmental management, occupational health and safety, regulatory compliance and asset integrity. Together, these systems support the consistent delivery of reliable, safe and sustainable transport infrastructure.
Maximising Asset Availability
We closely monitor asset performance to maintain seamless 
toll operations and high network availability. We capture real-time data and leverage automated reconciliation to improve the accuracy, efficiency and transparency of toll transactions.  
Digitally-enabled Toll Operations
We have strengthened toll operations through FASTag, 
RFID-enabled systems and advanced toll management platforms across our plazas. FASTag penetration exceeds 97%, enabling faster, contactless transactions while reducing congestion, vehicle idling, emissions, cash handling and manual intervention.Integrated digital platforms support real-time traffic and revenue monitoring, accurate and tamper-resistant collections, faster lane clearance and improved toll throughput. These capabilities enhance financial control, asset utilisation and commuter experience while advancing our alignment with national infrastructure priorities, including Gati Shakti, Bharatmala and the National Logistics Policy.
Building Resilient and Sustainable Assets
We integrate resource efficiency and operational resilience 
across the infrastructure lifecycle through:
 Water conservation and recycling at project sites
 Solar-powered digital tolling systems
 RFID-enabled toll management for faster vehicle movement and reduced congestion
 Continued investment in physical and digital infrastructure to support connected and sustainable mobilityInfrastructure Beyond Roads
Sindhudurg Airport
Marking our entry into multimodal infrastructure, we developed Sindhudurg Airport near the Goa-Maharashtra border through IRB Sindhudurg Airport Private Limited. The airport is fully operational for scheduled and non-scheduled commercial flights and provides comprehensive infrastructure support for domestic and chartered services.
Designed as a 24×7, all-weather IFR facility, the airport 
supports day-and-night operations and has published RNP approach procedures. Its six parking bays can accommodate Code C aircraft, including the B737 MAX and A320 family, with provision for night parking.
Strategically located, Sindhudurg Airport serves as an 
efficient and cost-effective gateway to the Konkan region, including Goa. It also supports our long-term strategy to expand multimodal logistics capabilities, with potential future integration across freight corridors and road, rail and air transport networks.Key Features
 2,500-metre runway, extendable to 3,400 metres 
 Six aircraft parking bays, expandable to 15 
 Dedicated fuel farm 
 Passenger handling capacity of 2 Mn annually 
 Peak-hour capacity of 200 arriving and 200 departing passengers, extendable to 400 each 
 Parking for 100 cars and 10 buses, with scope for expansion 
 Substantial land available for future commercial development

Operations

Sustainability is also integrated into our technology
